reading.synopsis: Ten-year-old Tony Rossi, born on the colonized planet of the insectile, hard-shelled Pas-udeti (dismissively called 'beetles' by Terrans), has never seen Earth and has grown up playing with Pas-udeti children in the city of Karnet, working alongside them on a model spaceport. His father, a former fleet officer bitter about a century-long war of Terran conquest, listens obsessively to war news from the distant Orion front, where Terra has held dominance since defeating the Pas-udeti a hundred years earlier. On what seems an ordinary visit to Karnet, Tony finds his usual playmates cold and withdrawn; word arrives that for the first time in a century, the Pas-udeti fleet has turned the Terran flank and is winning. His childhood friend B'prith, transformed by the news into an enemy rather than a playmate, spits the slur 'white-grub' in his face and leads a mob that stones Tony and destroys his robotic guardian (EEP) before a Terran scout ship rescues him. That evening, Tony's father — his earlier bluster gone — quietly admits to his wife and son what he has apparently known for a long time: Terra took this world by force, is now losing the century-long war it started, and will spend the coming centuries in slow, grinding retreat back toward Sol, the roles of conqueror and conquered finally reversing after a hundred years.

structure.form: short story in three movements: domestic normalcy, the turning point witnessed firsthand, the father's confession
movements: Breakfast at the Rossi household, establishing Tony's colonial childhood, his father's bitterness about the war, and casual Terran contempt for the Pas-udeti ('beetles').
Tony's trip into Karnet, his growing unease, and the mob violence that erupts the moment news arrives that the tide of the war has turned.
The family's aftermath conversation, in which Joe Rossi finally admits Terra's century-long occupation was theft and that its coming defeat is deserved.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Tony throughout the middle section, so the reader experiences the friendship's collapse from inside a child's uncomprehending shock rather than from an adult's already-cynical vantage.
structure.central_device: A child's friendship used as the precise instrument for measuring a century-long colonial injustice — the friendship's total, instant destruction the moment military fortune reverses demonstrates that it was never insulated from the occupation underlying it.

characters.name: Tony Rossi
characters.note: Genuinely does not understand, until his friends explain it to him directly, that his entire life has been lived on 'stolen ground' — his shock is the story's emotional center precisely because his affection for his Pas-udeti friends was real.

characters.name: Joe Rossi
characters.note: His opening bluster and racial contempt ('beetles,' 'white-grub'-inverting insults) curdle by the story's end into a resigned, honest admission that Terra's century of conquest was theft, and that the coming retreat is just.

characters.name: B'prith
characters.note: Explains the friendship's collapse in explicitly political rather than personal terms — 'it's not my fault, either' — before leading the mob that destroys Tony's robot guardian and nearly kills him.

characters.name: The young Pas-udeti female
characters.note: The story's one moment of cross-species solidarity that survives the day's violence — she tries, carefully and without fully explaining why, to warn Tony away from Karnet before the news breaks.

settings.name: The Terran settlement
settings.note: A cluster of pressurized housing units on a hostile, alien-atmosphere world, entirely dependent on technology (pump units, oxygen taps, EEP guardian robots) for survival — the literal fragility of the colonial presence made physical.

settings.name: Karnet
settings.note: The Pas-udeti city where Tony has played since childhood, its dust-proof envelope and ancient civilization presented with genuine specificity and dignity rather than as generic alien backdrop.

motifs: A slur ('beetle') revealed to derive from the very star (Betelgeuse) the occupied system orbits — colonial language embedded in the coloniality itself
A child's friendship as the precise instrument measuring the total collapse of an unjust peace the instant military fortune reverses
A father's bitter bluster giving way, once the danger is past, to a quiet, unqualified admission of guilt
Technology (the EEP robot) as the fragile guarantor of colonial safety, destroyed the moment the underlying power balance shifts
A century-long occupation's ending measured in the same currency as its beginning — force, invasion, retreat
reading.significance: Palmer groups this story with 'Martians Come in Clouds' as sharing a specific opening device — an angry scene between a hard-boiled father and his child — and situates both within a broader catalogue of 1950s Dick stories using domestic anger as an entry point into larger political and cosmic themes. What makes this story distinct within that catalogue is its refusal to let either side hold the moral high ground cleanly: Tony's friendship with the Pas-udeti children is genuine and its destruction is a real loss, while the story is equally clear that the friendship existed only within, and was always secretly bounded by, an occupation that both children's fathers understood better than the children did. Joe Rossi's late confession — that this was theft, and that the coming defeat is deserved — lands with force precisely because the story spent its first half establishing him as an unreflective bigot.
reading.closing_note: Joe Rossi's closing vow — 'we'll give them a run for their money... all the way back, every inch' — is delivered in the same breath as his admission that the retreat is deserved, refusing to resolve the contradiction between accepting defeat as just and still intending to resist it.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a century-long colonial occupation whose justice or injustice is measured directly through the collapse of a child's cross-species friendship the instant military fortune reverses
a genuinely dignified, non-monstrous depiction of an alien civilization and culture, contrasted against casual Terran racial contempt
